name: Hana Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to AI firms, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don’t sell anything or campaign. What you share is confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I’m Hana Patel, 27, and I lead a line crew for an electricity company. We meet at the south depot, check the permit and weather, then drive out to inspect poles or repair faults; I’m usually the one who signs off the crew’s return notes.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about it, and what is hardest?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like being able to point to a repaired line at the end of a shift, and I like that my crew trusts me with safety calls. The wet mornings are hard, but I’m paid a typical wage and have a few months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau: Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say a form-filling tool can tidy the return notes, but it can’t see whether a pole is leaning after a storm. We still walk the route before I sign off a repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the notes may take less time, while the crew keeps doing the same inspections and call-outs. My pay and savings feel steady in this small-change picture, though I still keep money for the car and rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d check the tool’s return note against our paper permit for a month before I let the crew rely on it. I’d keep the usual rota and continue my regular savings transfer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm because I don’t expect this tool to reduce the physical work. I would still rather check a neat form twice than discover a missing isolation note at the pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if it left out a repair detail?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d compare it with the crew’s field notes and call dispatch if the details didn’t match. I would keep the paper copy in the truck until we had checked the new process properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you spend any of your savings to buy a tool for the crew?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, that belongs to the company and it should pay for its equipment. I’d keep my savings for the ordinary things I already plan for, like rent and a car repair.

say: I’d say forms can tidy **return notes**, but they cannot inspect a storm-damaged pole.
I’d still walk the route before signing off **a repair**.
think: I think the crew keeps doing **inspections and call-outs** in this small-change picture.
My pay and savings feel steady, and I keep money for **rent and the car**.
do: Check the **return note** against the paper permit for a month.
Keep the **usual rota** and continue my regular savings transfer.
feel: I feel **calm about work**, while keeping normal bills in mind.
S0.quote: I feel calm because I don’t expect this tool to reduce the physical work.
fieldNote: Hana separates **tidier records** from the physical walk that confirms a repair at the actual work site.
Typical pay and **a few months saved** make the limited change manageable.

steps.text: Check return notes against paper permits during the first month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption: Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say scheduling software can arrange routine work orders, but we have to check the site before sending a crew. I’d ask management to explain what the new system changes in our lead duties.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I handle some planning and record checks, so I can see those parts shrinking. I think the physical jobs continue for a while, but I don’t know whether the company will keep the same number of crew leads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d let the experienced dispatcher show us the new schedule system, then compare a week of routes against our call-out log. I’d keep my field inspection skills current and ask for a written description of any changed lead role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m uneasy because it could affect part of my job, though I have time to see what our employer actually does. My savings give me some space, but I would not ignore a reduction in hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask before approving a route made by the new system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask how it handles a road closure and a crew’s qualification before it sends the order. A route can look efficient on a screen and still be wrong for the people and equipment available.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you assume a nearby utility would hire you if your lead role changed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn’t assume that, even though there are some similar employers within commuting distance. I’d ask about real openings and pay before deciding whether I could make a move.

say: I’d say software can arrange **work orders**, but crews check each site.
I’d ask management what changes in **our lead duties**.
think: I think **planning and record checks** in my role could shrink.
I don’t know whether the company will keep the same number of **crew leads**.
do: Compare a week of routes with the **call-out log** after dispatcher training.
Keep **field inspection skills** current and request a written role description.
Check **real vacancies and pay** before considering a move.
feel: I feel **uneasy**, because some duties may shrink but I have time to watch.
S1.quote: A route can look efficient on a screen and still be wrong for the people and equipment available.
fieldNote: She identifies **planning exposure** but does not assume all crew positions disappear.
Her cushion supports patience while she asks for **written role details** before a possible reduction in hours.

steps.text: Compare new routes against the call-out log with a dispatcher
Maintain the regular savings transfer while hours remain stable
Wait for written role changes and actual vacancy details

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028: Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say our planning, work records and fault diagnosis are exposed when AGI arrives in 2028. The robot date comes around 2031, so a few years remain for hands-on work, but I wouldn’t call that a permanent job guarantee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead paperwork could disappear first, and later robots could take some of our line work. I have a few months saved and some other utilities nearby, but I still don’t know how many jobs would be open.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d use the two years to earn an electrical safety trainer qualification if the company provides paid course time. In 2029 I’d apply for actual trainer openings and check how much is hands-on, since lesson planning and diagnosis are exposed too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious about my future role, but I can use my savings and start a qualification before the change. I would be much more worried if there were no time to prepare at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your partner about the course and the savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d explain that I want to use work hours for a recognized qualification rather than pay for a promise. I’d keep enough of our savings for household bills in case the course does not lead to a vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the trainer job be protected after full AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I can’t call training protected because AGI can write lesson plans and diagnose faults. I’d see a real trainer opening as one possible bridge, not a safe career after 2028.

say: I’d say **planning, records and diagnosis** are exposed in 2028.
I wouldn’t treat the later robot date as a **job guarantee**.
think: I think my **lead paperwork** could disappear first, with field work exposed later.
I have **some savings** and nearby utilities, but I don’t know which jobs will be open.
do: Earn a recognized **electrical safety trainer qualification** with paid course time.
Apply for actual trainer vacancies in **2029** and check their duties.
Keep **household savings** available for bills if no post appears.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but I can prepare with a modest financial buffer.
S2.quote: I’d see a real trainer opening as one possible bridge, not a safe career after 2028.
fieldNote: Hana names exposure in **lead paperwork** and later field work, without assuming all jobs vanish.
Her response uses **savings** while treating trainer vacancies as uncertain.

steps.text: Complete a recognized electrical safety trainer qualification
Apply to actual trainer vacancies in 2029 after checking duties

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031: Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say five years gives us time to learn the company’s procedure and ask what crew roles will change. I’d still expect AGI to take planning and diagnosis by 2031, and robots to reach physical work in 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can finish training more carefully than in the two-year case and keep building my cushion. I still think my lead paperwork is exposed, and a nearby vacancy is not the same as a guaranteed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d get the training plan and recognized certificate in writing before I commit my evenings. In 2032 I’d look at trainer or inspection posts, then compare the wages and tasks with my current line role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’m anxious, though five years gives me time to make a careful choice. I would not move for a vague promise, because deposits and travel would use a real share of my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you trust an advertised certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask the company which qualification it recognizes and whether its trainers have actual openings. I’d also speak to a worker who took the course before I rearranged my shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move for a confirmed trainer job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d consider it if the pay covered rent and travel and my partner agreed. I’d keep enough savings to handle the move and a gap before the first pay.

say: I’d say five years gives time to learn **company procedures** and ask about roles.
I’d still expect thinking tasks to change in 2031 and physical work in **2034**.
think: I can finish training carefully and **build my cushion**.
I know a nearby vacancy is not a **guaranteed offer** for me.
do: Get a written **training plan** before enrolling in the recognized certificate.
Compare trainer and inspection posts in **2032** with current pay and tasks.
Consider moving only when the offer covers rent and **travel costs**.
feel: I feel **anxious but deliberate**, with time to compare real choices.
S3.quote: I still think my lead paperwork is exposed, and a nearby vacancy is not the same as a guaranteed offer.
fieldNote: She uses the warning to **verify course value** and compare wages before changing roles.
Relocation remains conditional on **an offer** and agreement from her partner.

steps.text: Get the recognized safety training plan in writing
Compare actual trainer vacancies and wages in 2032
Move only for an offer covering rent and travel
Preserve savings for the moving deposit and first-pay gap

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036: Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years gives me time to finish training and ask the company for a transition plan. I still expect planning and records to change in 2036, with robots reaching line work around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have more time to save and consider another role without rushing out of a job that pays my bills. But I won’t call training or inspection permanently safe when AGI can do the planning and diagnosis.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d complete a recognized safety course in stages and keep my existing savings transfer, aiming for a larger reserve. In 2037 I’d compare actual vacancies and pay before deciding whether to apply or stay with the line crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy rather than safe, because the dates still reach my job if I stay in it long enough. Ten years lets me make a measured plan and use my current savings instead of panicking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you change about your routine this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d reserve one evening for the course and keep my regular savings transfer. I’d also ask the crew supervisor for a written update every year, rather than make a sudden move based on a headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the course lead to a permanently safe career?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, a trainer or inspector still plans, writes and diagnoses, so I wouldn’t treat that work as safe after full AGI. I’d see it as one option to review alongside the line jobs still available before 2039.

say: I’d say ten years gives me time to train and **request a transition plan**.
I expect planning to change in 2036 and line work to face robots in **2039**.
think: I can build savings and consider a role without **rushing away** from my wage.
I won’t call training or inspection permanently **safe** after AGI.
do: Complete a recognized **safety course** in stages.
Continue my **savings transfer** and aim for a larger reserve.
Compare real vacancies and wages in **2037** before applying.
feel: I feel **uneasy but prepared**, since I have time to plan.
S4.quote: Ten years lets me make a measured plan and use my current savings instead of panicking.
fieldNote: A longer horizon supports **measured preparation**, while she recognizes eventual exposure in her current role.
She treats training as an **option to compare**, not guaranteed protection.

steps.text: Complete the recognized line-safety course in stages
Continue the existing savings transfer toward a larger reserve
Wait for annual staffing information before deciding whether to apply

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I’d have little time before planning changes, then three years until the robot date. Paid training, clear information about staffing, and enough time to compare actual vacancies would help me prepare responsibly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks a new system’s safety instructions against what crews see outside. I’m willing to learn a proven process, but someone must answer for a bad instruction before it reaches a pole.

headlineQuote: I’m willing to learn a proven process, but someone must answer for a bad instruction before it reaches a pole.
portrait: Hana is a **27-year-old crew lead** who values clear safety calls and visible repairs.
She earns a typical wage and has **a few months saved**.
She accepts tested tools but wants **written procedures** before changing practice.
More warning gives her time to **train and compare roles**, without making future jobs certain.
biggestWorry: AGI by **2028** leaves little time before planning changes and robots arrive in 2031.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training**, clear staffing information and time to compare vacancies would help her prepare.
